sentences.text: She went up on the twenty-sixth of February.

It had been agreed, in the way things were agreed there — which is to say that nobody had ever said to Lise *you are doing it*, and yet by the end of January there was no other candidate and everyone had stopped mentioning alternatives.
She was not the obvious person.
She was twelve.

But the valley had seven households left in it and four of those were people over seventy, and of the rest there was Lise, her brother who was six, and the Marek boys who were nineteen and twenty-two and who had both said no in a way that closed the subject.
It took her two hours and forty minutes to get up to the shoulder, in good weather, with a flask.
Her father walked with her as far as the second gate, which was as far as anybody was allowed to come, and stood there while she went on up.
She did not look back until the bend, and when she did he was still there, and she was extremely annoyed with herself for looking.
Above the second gate the path stops being a path.

It is a line of slightly-less-bad ground across a slope of loose grey stone, and in February it has snow on it in the hollows and ice under the snow, and Lise went up it in her brother's crampons, which were too big, taking the long zigzag her father had made her promise to take.

The ermine was on the wall by the ruined byre, which is where Nikolai had said she would be, and she sat up when Lise came round the corner and looked at her with the egg-sized nothing glowing in her jaws.
Lise had thought about it for four months and had prepared nothing, on purpose, because everyone had told her that preparing was the mistake.
She said: "Please can you put it down." Nothing happened.
She said it again, and then she said it a third time in dialect rather than in school German, in case that was the thing.
The ermine sat on the wall and looked at her and did not put it down.
Lise stayed up there for about an hour.
She sat on the wall herself, at a distance, and she talked.
She said all the reasonable things: that the valley needed the grass, that the Hofers had run out of hay, that her father's back would not stand another month of it.
She said, at one point, feeling humiliated, that she was sorry she was not Nikolai.
The ermine washed her face with one front paw, which is a thing they can do while holding something, and which Lise found extremely rude.
Then she went along the wall and off into the rocks.
Lise came down the mountain in the dark, badly, having stayed too long, and was met halfway by her father with a torch who did not ask her anything at all until they were inside.
When they were inside, and she had her boots off, he asked her whether she was cold, and she said no, and he said good, and that was the entire conversation about it.

She heard him on the telephone to Nikolai's daughter later, through the floor, saying it had not worked, in a voice that was not disappointed at all — and she lay in bed working out that he had never expected it to, and that he had not said so, and that both of those had probably been kindnesses.
